pr.title: match lowering: Lower bindings in a predictable order
pr.description:
After the recent refactorings, we can now lower bindings in a truly predictable order. The order in https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/pull/120214 was an improvement but not very clear. With this PR, we lower bindings from left to right, with the special case that `x @ pat` is traversed as `pat @ x` (i.e. `x` is lowered after any bindings in `pat`). 

This description only applies in the absence of or-patterns. Or-patterns make everything complicated, because the binding place depends on the subpattern. Until I have a better idea I leave them to be handled in whatever weird order arises from today's code.

r? @matthewjasper
pr.author: Nadrieril

processing.reason: The historical rewrite only changes (a) compile-time borrow-check acceptance for `x @ (A(a) | A(a))` with a non-`Copy` `A`, yielding E0382, and (b) semantically inert MIR ordering (`StorageLive`/assignment/`StorageDead` order and `switchInt` test order). The known-bug program does not compile, so it cannot be a pair of Miri-passing functions. The MIR-order changes keep identical value assignments and only reorder pure operations, so they cannot produce different observable numeric/boolean results. Encoding the move-order bug via `Option::take` sentinels, order-logging, or similar would be a manufactured interpreter rather than the actual historical transformation, and the instructions require both implementations to pass Miri while exhibiting a genuine source-grounded semantic difference. No such runtime counterexample exists for this PR.

analysis.originalLogic: `Builder::simplify_match_pairs` in `compiler/rustc_mir_build/src/build/matches/simplify.rs` used a repeated-simplification loop with an `accumulated_bindings` vector: each pass collected newly found irrefutable bindings into `candidate_bindings`, then prepended them to the previously accumulated bindings and swapped the vectors. The source comment states the rule explicitly: "We can't just reverse the binding order, because we must preserve pattern-order" and "Our rule then is: deepest-first," with "and bindings at the same depth stay in source order." It also says: "To do this, every time around the loop we prepend the newly found bindings to the" and "bindings we already had." Unsimplifiable match pairs were pushed into `simplified_match_pairs` and only at the end swapped back into `match_pairs`. This produced a binding order driven by pattern depth rather than a clear source-order traversal, and produced a match-pair/test order that differed from the new implementation.
analysis.incorrectTransformation: The transformation being replaced lowers pattern bindings in depth-first/deepest-first order (with same-depth bindings in source order) instead of left-to-right source order, and, in the direction that remains incorrect for or-patterns, lowers the `x` in `x @ pat` before the bindings inside `pat`. The PR's new rule is: "We therefore lower bindings from left-to-right, except we lower the `x` in `x @ pat`" followed by "after any bindings in `pat`. This doesn't work for or-patterns: the current structure of" and "match lowering forces us to lower bindings inside or-patterns last." The incorrect ordering is directly documented by the new known-bug test: "// The or-pattern bindings are lowered after `x`, which triggers the error." The test program `let x @ (A(a) | A(a)) = A(10);` is rejected with E0382 "use of moved value", while the same bindings placed as `let (x @ A(a) | x @ A(a)) = A(10);` are accepted because `x` is lowered after the inner `a` binding in each alternative. Thus the historically incorrect transformation is: when an `@` binding encloses subpattern bindings (especially or-pattern bindings), emit the outer binding's move before the inner bindings, invalidating them. The patch does not fix this or-pattern case; it records it with `//@ known-bug: unknown`.
analysis.inputDomain: Rust MIR match lowering for patterns that contain multiple bindings, `@` bindings, or-patterns, and tuple/struct/enum subpatterns. The borrow-check consequence appears only when bindings are by-value (bind-by-move) and the matched type is not `Copy`, so moving the outer `@` binding consumes the value needed by later inner bindings. The MIR-order consequence appears in ordinary patterns too, e.g. tuple-typed matches over `Option` fields where `StorageLive`/assignment/`StorageDead` order and the order of `switchInt` tests are visible in `EarlyOtherwiseBranch` and `SimplifyCfg` MIR dumps. The PR description explicitly limits the predictable-order rule: "This description only applies in the absence of or-patterns."
analysis.summary: Historical match-lowering refactor that makes binding lowering deterministic: bindings are lowered left-to-right, except `x @ pat` is traversed as `pat @ x`, so the `@` binding is lowered after bindings in its subpattern. The rule intentionally does not apply to or-patterns, where the structure of match lowering still forces or-pattern bindings to be lowered last; a new UI test records that `let x @ (A(a) | A(a)) = A(10);` produces E0382 while `let (x @ A(a) | x @ A(a)) = A(10);` works. The patch updates `EarlyOtherwiseBranch` and `SimplifyCfg` MIR expectation dumps to the new ordering. This is an optimization/refactor for predictable ordering, not a confirmed fix of the or-pattern bug.
analysis.trigger: Triggered when a match/lowering candidate contains several bindings and the lowering order is observable: (a) an `@` binding around subpattern bindings, especially around an or-pattern, where lowering the outer binding first moves a non-`Copy` value before the inner bindings are established; (b) ordinary tuple/`Option` patterns where the old deepest-first accumulation emitted `StorageLive`/assignments/`StorageDead` in a different order and tested match pairs in a different order than the new left-to-right traversal. In the `exponential_or.match_tuple` `SimplifyCfg` dump the first test moves from a `_1.2` discriminant test to a `_1.0` `switchInt`, i.e. the tuple field `_1.0` is now tested before `_1.2`.
preconditions: The matched value has a non-`Copy` type and bindings are by-value/bind-by-move, so moving at one binding invalidates later bindings (the test uses `struct A(u32);`).
An `@` binding encloses subpattern bindings, and for the known-bug case the subpattern is an or-pattern: `let x @ (A(a) | A(a)) = A(10);`.

For MIR-order checks, the test must observe exact statement order (`StorageLive`, assignment, `StorageDead`) or exact `switchInt` ordering, as in the `EarlyOtherwiseBranch` diffs and `exponential_or.match_tuple.SimplifyCfg-initial.after.mir`.
The predictable-order rule is only claimed for patterns without or-patterns; or-pattern binding places depend on the chosen subpattern.
pitfalls: Do not treat the reordered `StorageLive`/`StorageDead` hunks as a semantic change: the `EarlyOtherwiseBranch` diffs keep the same value assignments (`_8` from `_3.0`, `_9` from `_3.1`) and only exchange their order.

The outer patch edits test expectations; a retained test name or old comment does not show that `EarlyOtherwiseBranch` or `SimplifyCfg` is itself wrong. The changed hunks are decoded MIR input/output ordering.

Do not conflate the borrow-check/move error (the known-bug or-pattern test) with the harmless MIR statement reordering in the `EarlyOtherwiseBranch` dumps; they are separate observable consequences of binding order.

Do not claim this PR fixes the or-pattern bug: the added test is marked `//@ known-bug: unknown`, and the PR states `This doesn't work for or-patterns` and leaves them `to be handled in whatever weird order arises from today's code`.
Do not generalize left-to-right ordering to or-patterns: the description says `This description only applies in the absence of or-patterns.`
Do not model `x @ pat` as plain source order; the intended order is `x @ pat` traversed as `pat @ x`, so the outer binding is lowered after inner bindings in the non-or-pattern case.

The `SimplifyCfg` hunk changes match-test order (a `_1.0` `switchInt` before the `_1.2` discriminant), not merely binding statements; verify which order the expectation actually encodes before attributing a failure to `SimplifyCfg` itself.
No compiler was built and no execution or reproduction was performed; conclusions are from the supplied patch, test source, and decoded MIR diffs only.
analysis.testStrategy: Use two complementary focused strategies. (1) Borrow-check/UI differential: create two programs identical except for `@`/or-pattern placement, using a non-`Copy` type: `let x @ (A(a) | A(a)) = A(10);` must fail borrowck with E0382 (known-bug, `//@ known-bug: unknown`), while `let (x @ A(a) | x @ A(a)) = A(10);` must compile and allow `x.0` and `a` to be read. Keep the surrounding assertions (`assert!(x.0 == 10); assert!(a == 10);`) so the move invalidation is exercised. (2) MIR-order expectations: add/update mir-opt tests whose dumps assert the exact order of `StorageLive`/assignment/`StorageDead` for multiple bindings (the `early_otherwise_branch*.EarlyOtherwiseBranch.diff` files across opt1/opt2/opt3, the 3-element-tuple and 68867 `try_sum` cases, and `early_otherwise_branch_noopt.noopt1`). Also include a `SimplifyCfg` test such as `exponential_or.match_tuple.SimplifyCfg-initial.after.mir` that asserts the order of the `switchInt` tests; the changed expectation shows `_1.0` tested first. Verify that within each reordered hunk the moved assignments still write the same places from the same sources, so the test distinguishes ordering-only changes from wrong value propagation. No execution was performed here; treat these as test designs.
